sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html:
Show entry, magazine submission, jury applications, and the family archive all run on the same photograph. Phone cameras guess at reds and stretch texture; a quilt photographed properly looks on screen the way it looks in your hands.

Every session delivers web-sized images for forms and print-ready files for catalogs, both color-checked against the quilt on the wall before they leave the studio.

sections.heading: How a session runs
sections.html:
Bring the quilt loose, not pinned to a rod, and give it ten minutes to relax out of the car. Squares go on the wall with pins that have never met a quilt before, the level does the arguing, and each shot is checked on the monitor with you standing there.

You pick keepers on the spot. Nothing is delivered that you did not approve, and nothing is retouched that the quilt did not do.

items.q: Can you photograph a quilt that hangs badly?
items.a: Almost every quilt hangs badly until it is pinned properly. Bring it; the wall and the steamer will handle the rest.

items.q: Do I get the raw files?
items.a: You get the finished files, print and web. Raw files are the negative and the darkroom, and they stay in the studio like negatives did.
King quilts shoot in two passes and are stitched square on the bench. Bring a friend to help drape and it takes ten extra minutes.

sections.heading: How a guild day runs
sections.html:
The studio brings the backdrop, the stands, and the light to your meeting hall. Members book ten-minute slots through the guild, quilts go up in show order, and everyone leaves with files by the weekend. The guild keeps a share of the day as a fundraiser, which has paid for more than one speaker's mileage.

Show days work the same way at 7 a.m., before the doors, while the hang is fresh and the halls are empty.

items.quote: Thirty-one member quilts photographed in one morning, and the guild treasury gained two speakers' fees.
items.author: A program chair

sections.title: Behind the camera
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: A product photographer who married a quilter and finally found subjects that hold still and mean something.

sections.html:
Ten years photographing things nobody loved: gadget packaging, rental furniture, one memorable year of socks. A favor for my mother-in-law's quilt guild turned into the only work where the subject has a name, a maker, and an opinion about which corner is the good one.

Every quilt is handled like a loan from a museum, because to somebody in the room it is one. White gloves are not pretension; they are what the quilts taught me.

items.quote: The photograph caught the quilting lines better than I could see them from the saddle of making it.
items.author: A first-time entrant
